blocks.orig: QUICK FACTS ABOUT THE GREAT WILDEBEEST MIGRATION
blocks.html: Quick facts about the Great Wildebeest Migration

blocks.orig: The Great Wildebeest Migration is one of the largest land mammal migrations in the world, with almost two million animals crossing the Tanzanian plains each year.
blocks.html: With close to two million animals moving across the plains of Tanzania every year, the Great Wildebeest Migration ranks among the biggest land mammal migrations on earth.

blocks.orig: Although named after wildebeests, which make the majority of animals, the migrating herds also include zebras, topi, gazelles, and other animals.
blocks.html: Wildebeest give the migration its name and make up most of the animals, but zebras, topi, gazelles and other species travel with the herds too.

blocks.orig: The migration typically begins in December and lasts until November, although its beginning depends on the start of the rainy season in Tanzania.
blocks.html: As a rule the migration kicks off in December and continues through to November, though exactly when it starts hinges on the arrival of Tanzania’s rainy season.

blocks.orig: The herds cover approximately 1,000 kilometers during the migration cycle.
blocks.html: Over a full migration cycle the herds travel roughly 1,000 kilometres.

blocks.orig: Up to 250,000 wildebeests are killed by predators during the migration.
blocks.html: As many as 250,000 wildebeest fall victim to predators in the course of the migration.

blocks.orig: Migrating wildebeests divide into herds of hundreds of thousands of animals.
blocks.html: On the move, the wildebeest split up into herds of hundreds of thousands of animals.

blocks.orig: WHEN AND WHERE IS THE GREAT WILDEBEEST MIGRATION?
blocks.html: Where and when does the Great Wildebeest Migration happen?

blocks.orig: Here’s the trick – the exact timing of the Serengeti wildebeest migration depends upon the rainfall patterns each year. This makes predicting where and when the migration begins. It’s something not even wildebeests know!
blocks.html: Here is the catch: the precise timing of the Serengeti wildebeest migration follows the rainfall patterns of each year. That makes forecasting where and when it begins tricky. Even the wildebeest don’t know!

blocks.orig: Due to climate changes, the rainy seasons haven’t been occurring regularly, nor are they easily predictable. That’s also why the migration has been thrown out of synch in recent years.
blocks.html: Because of climate change the rainy seasons no longer arrive on a regular schedule, nor are they easy to predict. That is also why the migration has slipped out of sync in recent years.

blocks.orig: However, thanks to our experienced Your Tanzania Trip guides, we are able to make a fairly accurate prediction. This is one of the main reasons why our Tanzania safaris are so popular for everyone who wants to see this spectacle with their own eyes.
blocks.html: Still, with the help of our experienced Your Tanzania Trip guides we can forecast it fairly accurately. It is one of the main reasons our Tanzania safaris are so popular with people who want to see this spectacle with their own eyes.

blocks.orig: The migration typically begins in late November or early December, when migrating herds arrive in the southern parts of Tanzania’s Serengeti National Park in the Ndutu area.
blocks.html: Usually the migration gets under way in late November or early December, when the moving herds reach the southern part of Tanzania’s Serengeti National Park around Ndutu.

blocks.orig: When in the Serengeti, the animals are free to move wherever they want. It’s a truly magnificent sight of almost two million wildebeests and zebras dispersed throughout Tanzania’s plains, enjoying fresh and nutritious grasses.
blocks.html: Once in the Serengeti, the animals roam wherever they like. It is a truly majestic sight: almost two million wildebeest and zebras spread out across the Tanzanian plains, feeding on fresh, nutritious grass.

blocks.orig: In February, the calving season begins, with half a million calves born on these southern plains. You can also see a lot of predators at this time, who are all waiting for easy prey.
blocks.html: The calving season starts in February, when some half a million calves arrive on these southern plains. Predators are plentiful then too, all hoping for an easy meal.

blocks.orig: Around April, the herds head for the central and western part of the Serengeti in search of fresh, long grass. The rains start, and the mating season begins.
blocks.html: Come April the herds set off for the central and western Serengeti to find fresh, long grass. With the arrival of the rains, the mating season begins.

blocks.orig: In May and June, the herds of wildebeests and zebras migrate further north to get ready for the dangerous Grumeti River crossing full of giant crocodiles.
blocks.html: In May and June the wildebeest and zebra herds push further north, preparing for the perilous Grumeti River crossing, where huge crocodiles lie in wait.

blocks.orig: It’s a scary sight as you watch thousands of these magnificent creatures struggle against the forces of nature and predators. Unfortunately, not all animals survive the crossing.
blocks.html: It is a frightening thing to watch: thousands of these magnificent animals battling the forces of nature and predators. Sadly, not every animal makes it across.

blocks.orig: The survivors continue their journey, with some herds heading through the Grumeti Game Reserve and Ikorongo Game Reserve while others choose the path piercing through the heart of the Serengeti National Park.
blocks.html: Those that survive carry on, some herds passing through the Grumeti Game Reserve and Ikorongo Game Reserve, others taking the route straight through the heart of Serengeti National Park.

blocks.orig: From July till September, you’ll find the herds around the Mara River, which they need to cross to get to Kenya. The sights are impressive as well as dramatic around this time. The fast-flowing water and crocodiles make this crossing extremely dangerous for the herds.
blocks.html: Between July and September the herds gather around the Mara River, which they must cross to reach Kenya. The scenes at this time are as dramatic as they are impressive: the fast current and the crocodiles make this crossing extremely dangerous for the herds.

blocks.orig: The Mara River crossing is the most serious obstacle during the migration, creating a spectacular yet often hair-raising spectacle of panic and confusion as herds consisting of hundreds of thousands of animals try to get through the gushing river.
blocks.html: The Mara River crossing is the toughest obstacle of the whole migration. It produces a spectacular and often hair-raising scene of panic and chaos as herds of hundreds of thousands of animals attempt to get through the raging water.

blocks.orig: Interestingly, in the last two years, almost two-thirds of the migration did not cross the Mara River since there was enough fresh grass left in the northern Serengeti.
blocks.html: Interestingly, during the past two years nearly two-thirds of the migration stayed put instead of crossing the Mara River, because the northern Serengeti still had enough fresh grass.

blocks.orig: From October till November, the wildebeest migration leaves the northern Serengeti and makes its way back to the southern part/Ndutu via the central Seronera region. The herds remain there until late November/early December, and the annual cycle starts all over again.
blocks.html: In October and November the wildebeest migration leaves the northern Serengeti and heads back south towards Ndutu through the central Seronera region. The herds stay there until late November/early December, when the yearly cycle begins again.
